heading: Five Colleges, One Associates Degree
subHeading: A young woman's solitary struggle to get through school
content: There was no one in my life to guide me around what college was about. I went to public school and viewed education as an end in itself. I didn't see it as an end to a means. Careers and financial planning were not things that my family thought much about. My parents had jobs and paid rent.  They, and thus I, were always at the mercy of the owners of things.

At the age of 18, I found myself at Oberlin College in Ohio. I earned my own way there with lots of hard work in high school and a scholarship and a summer job. I literally had to earn my own plane fare and make all the arrangements myself. My family wasn’t so much discouraging as clueless about why I was going to such an expensive and remote college. I didn’t really notice how hands-off my parents were being – when I told them the school expected them to provide a portion of the tuition not covered by my scholarship, they didn't say no, but they never said yes either. My assumption that they would share the burden turned out to be incorrect, so I was forced to take on all of the debt myself. In that first year, I racked up an amount that seemed to my limited experience to be beyond what was repayable in a lifetime. Pair that with culture shock, being far from home, and a good case of "what am I doing here?" I'll admit I had a super rough freshman year navigating all that plus some other serious issues that I wasn't ready to face at the time. So over the summer, I chickened out and decided to just stick with the job I had gotten to earn the cash to fly back the next year.  Do I wish that I'd stayed? Yes! But I'm not at all sure that I would have been able to make the most of the opportunity at that time. Getting to experience Oberlin was a gift I’m grateful to have had.

After a year or so at what should have been just a summer job, I realized it was a dead end, that my potential was for so much more, and enrolled in City College of San Francisco, then transferred to SF State, where I studied philosophy.  This time I was doing pretty well, but was soon wondering, again, how I was going to pay the bill for this education, and dropped out again.  Skip ahead 5 years. I'd managed to cobble together my own house cleaning business and was doing some warehouse work, and again got the itch to better live up to my potential and, a lifelong artist, started exploring my options at The Academy of Art. I signed up and started on a degree in illustration. This time I was in it to win. However, the debt I'd somehow avoided from my past attempts at college, caught up with me, and the loans were withdrawn, and I had to stop once again!

These early college experiences were not an entire loss, though. I acquired essential knowledge and valuable learning skills. I didn't understand the importance that was placed on the diploma – it was always the knowledge that I was after anyway, and I received plenty. Someone had sold me their old Super Mac for $100 to write papers with, but I kept getting distracted hacking the visual interface for hours on end. I realized that if I could break into the tech industry, I would have a career that wouldn't feel like work. I bought an O'Reilly book on HTML and started studying and building. Before long, a friend in the industry noticed my talent, and I was hired! It's been non-stop learning ever since.

Many years later during the crash of 2008, after having relocated to Rochester, NY to support my partner's aging parents, I found myself unable to find tech work. I dreamt of being able to support myself half-time at a "day job" and half with my (he)art work.  Seeing several job listings for part-time bookkeeper, I thought a community college degree in accounting would make that dream a reality. I managed to finish that 2-year degree with honors. Unfortunately, I found that accounting was not a good culture fit for me. By then, the economy was healing, I had built a network, and was able to resume my tech career.
